s: The weak acids give far less H⁺.
Most H⁺ means lowest pH: HCl.
t: Equal concentrations do not mean equal pH. The acids dissociate to different extents.
HCN has the smallest Ka, so it gives the least H⁺ and the highest pH.
Acetic acid is weak. Its pH is near 2.9, well above 1.0.
HF is the strongest of the weak acids but still only partly dissociates. Its pH is near 2.1.
c: Which of the four has the highest pH?
HCN, the acid with the smallest Ka.
gchem-b:GC_sw-e6.w: HCl is the only strong acid here. It dissociates completely, so [H⁺] = 0.10 M and pH = 1.0. The weak acids dissociate only partly and sit higher: HF about 2.1, CH₃COOH about 2.9, HCN about 5.2.

t: A quarter volt would need a far larger concentration ratio than 10 to 1.
This forgets n = 2. Dividing 0.0592 by 2 gives 0.030 V.
Zero is E°, not E. The concentration difference still drives a small voltage.
This multiplies by 2 instead of dividing by n = 2.
c: What is E if the dilute side is 0.010 M instead?
The ratio is 100, so E = 0.0296 × 2 = 0.059 V.

s: For addition, count **decimal places**, not sig figs.
5.6 has the fewest: one decimal place.
t: This drops to a whole number. 5.6 allows one decimal place.
Two decimal places is more than 5.6 supports.
This is the raw calculator value with no rounding.
The extra zero claims two decimal places. 5.6 allows one.
c: How should 10.1 + 2.345 be reported?
12.4, with one decimal place.

gchem-b:GC_ks-h1.w: Let s be the solubility. Then [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s, so Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³. That gives s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³ and s ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
t: This takes a square root, as for a 1 to 1 salt. Ag₂CrO₄ needs a cube root.
This reports Ksp itself as the solubility.
This is too large: 4s³ would come to 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰, not 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
This doubles Ksp. Solubility comes from a cube root.
c: What is [Ag⁺] in the saturated solution?

s: N₂ needs 3 × 0.357 = 1.07 mol H₂. There is 2.00.
t: H₂ is in excess: only 1.07 of its 2.00 mol are needed.
This just adds the two masses. One reactant runs out first.
H₂ is in excess, so it cannot limit.
17.0 g is a full mole of NH₃. Only 0.714 mol forms.
c: How many moles of H₂ are left over?

gchem-b:GC_en-e7.w: ΔH = sum of ΔHf° for products minus sum for reactants = [-394 + 2(-242)] - [-239 + 0] = -878 + 239 = -639 kJ.
t: This does not follow from the data. The products total -878 kJ and the reactant -239 kJ.
This counts one water. The equation has two.
This adds the reactant value instead of subtracting it, then flips the sign.
This has the right size and the wrong sign. Combustion releases heat.
c: Why does O₂ contribute nothing to the sum?
Its formation enthalpy is zero: it is an element in its standard state.

t: This swaps the abundances. The lighter isotope is the common one.
This is the lighter isotope alone. A quarter of the atoms are heavier.
This is the heavier isotope alone. Three quarters of the atoms are lighter.
This is a plain average of 35 and 37. The abundances are not equal.
c: An element is 50% mass 10 and 50% mass 11. What is its average mass?
What is the pH of 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M NaOH?
What is the volume at 2 atm if the temperature stays at 127 °C?

s: Added H⁺ reacts with **A⁻**, one for one.
There is 0.20 mol of A⁻ per liter.
So about 0.20 mol/L of H⁺ uses it up.
t: This is five times the conjugate base present.
This is a quarter of the A⁻. The buffer keeps working well past it.
This is the amount of HA, which sets the capacity for added base.
This adds HA and A⁻ together. Only A⁻ neutralizes acid.
c: About how much strong base can this buffer absorb?
About 0.10 mol/L, the amount of HA.

t: This has the right ratio but is not reduced. Divide the subscripts by 3.
This has one H per carbon. The data give two.
This is glucose, a molecular formula. The empirical formula is the simplest ratio.
This has the right ratio but is not reduced. Divide the subscripts by 2.
c: What is the empirical formula of C₆H₆?
CH.

t: This would need a water mole fraction of 0.80. It is 0.90.
This is pure water. A nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure.
This is the amount the pressure drops, not the new pressure.
This adds the drop. A nonvolatile solute lowers vapor pressure, never raises it.
c: What is the vapor pressure when the mole fraction of water is 0.50?
What is the volume at 2 atm?
Half as much: 12.3 L.

t: This would mean 10% dissociation. Then x² is 2.5 × 10⁻⁵, five times Ka × 0.05.
This is the square root of Ka alone. Multiply by 0.05 first.
This slips a power of ten: it is the root of 5.0 × 10⁻⁷.
Here x² is 2.0 × 10⁻⁶. The product Ka × 0.05 is 5.0 × 10⁻⁶.
c: What is the pH of this solution?
-log(2.2 × 10⁻³) is about 2.65.

s: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ gives solid white BaSO₄.
c: Which anion would you add to precipitate Ag⁺?
Chloride. AgCl is insoluble.
If the rate tripled over the same 10 K, would Eₐ be larger or smaller?
Larger. A bigger Eₐ makes the rate more sensitive to temperature.
How much reactant is left after 60 min?
Two half-lives: one quarter.

t: This is about twice the heating-only pressure of 1.25 atm. The added gas raises it by a fifth, not double.
This uses the Celsius ratio 100/25. Gas laws need kelvin: 373/298.
Heating a sealed gas and adding more both raise the pressure. It cannot fall.
Nothing here multiplies the pressure by more than five. Moles rise 20% and kelvin temperature 25%.
c: What is the pressure at 100 °C if no gas is added?

s: More reactant makes the bottom bigger.
The reaction runs forward until Q = K.
c: Some product is removed instead. Which way does the reaction run?
Forward. Q again falls below K.

s: Polar bonds cancel when the shape is **symmetric**.
CO₂, BF₃ and CCl₄ are symmetric with identical outer atoms.
CH₂Cl₂ has two H and two Cl.
Its bond dipoles do not cancel.
t: The two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
CH₂Cl₂ is polar, so not all four are nonpolar.
Four identical C-Cl dipoles on a tetrahedron cancel.
Three identical B-F dipoles at 120° cancel.
c: Is CHCl₃ polar?
Yes. One H and three Cl do not cancel.

s: Each molecule has **2 H atoms**: 4 mol H.
c: How many oxygen atoms are in the sample?
2 mol, or 1.2 × 10²⁴ atoms.

t: 24 is the count for nitrate. Chlorine brings 7 electrons, not 5.
This forgets the extra electron from the -1 charge.
This is two too many: 7 + 18 + 1 = 26.
32 is the count for perchlorate, which has four oxygens.
c: How many valence electrons are in NH₄⁺?

s: That H⁺ accepts an electron pair from the base.
Accepting a pair is the Lewis definition.
So every Brønsted acid is a Lewis acid.
t: BF₃ is a Lewis acid with no proton to donate.
They overlap: HCl fits both definitions.
Lewis theory applies in any solvent, water included.
Brønsted theory also works outside water, as in liquid ammonia.
c: Is AlCl₃ a Brønsted acid, a Lewis acid, or both?
A Lewis acid only. It accepts an electron pair and has no proton.

gchem-b:GC_gb-e5.w: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 40,000 J / 100 J/K = 400 K. Above 400 K the entropy term wins and the reaction is spontaneous.
t: At 1000 K, ΔG is -60 kJ: already well past the crossover.
At 300 K, ΔG is +10 kJ: not yet spontaneous.
At 200 K, ΔG is +20 kJ: not yet spontaneous.
At 500 K, ΔG is -10 kJ: already past the crossover.
c: What is ΔG at 400 K?
Zero. The system is at equilibrium.

So the temperature change reflects the reaction alone.
c: If heat leaks out during an exothermic run, is the measured ΔT too high or too low?
Too low.
